American universities are heading downwards in a spiral of self-delusion. They still talk about their commitment to excellence, their great achievements, their leadership of the world of science, but they lament the damage that President Trump has inflicted, is inflicting, or is about to inflict on them. As Harvard President Alan M. Garber wrote in a letter to the campus community this past spring:

The cold reality, however, is that American university research, particularly in the sciences, began to decline decades ago, and Trump had nothing to do with it. The decline was largely self-inflicted.

American higher education may not recognize its diminished status on the global stage. It enjoys the support of Western experts, administrators, and media, and fares exceptionally well in the annual lists of major international university rankings. But those rankers have glossed over a steady decline in quality.

Americans generally focus on the domestic rankings published by U.S. News and World Report, and maybe some business-school rankings, the Princeton Review, or even the alternative Washington Monthly rankings. When they look at global rankings, they usually see only the “big four”: the Shanghai Rankings (aka the Academic Ranking of World Universities); the U.S. News Best Global Universities; the QS; and the Times Higher Education World University Rankings, the latter two of which are published in the United Kingdom.

The “big four” usually have good news for the United States and the West. Harvard leads in the overall rankings for U.S. News and the Shanghai rankings, MIT leads for QS, and Oxford leads for Times Higher Education (THE). The top 10 in each of these rankings is made up of American and British universities, apart from the National University of Singapore and ETH Zürich, which appear in the QS rankings.

But this is a deceptive story. Those four rankings are not the entirety of the global-ranking scene. There are a dozen others, generally published by universities or research centers, that rely on publicly available sources rather than surveys or data submitted by institutions. They get little publicity and run on limited budgets, with a lot of the hard work done by graduate students or interns. They include the Center for World University Rankings, published in the United Arab Emirates; the National Taiwan University Rankings; the Leiden Ranking, in the Netherlands; University Ranking by Academic Performance, based in Türkiye; the Round University Ranking, in Georgia; and SCImago Institutions Rankings, in Spain.

These less globally prominent rankings systems have a precarious existence. They are underfunded and occasionally face closure and consolidation. They have differing methodologies, but they converge on a common narrative: the fall of the American university, and the rise of the Chinese research university.

The Leiden Ranking is produced by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies at Leiden University. It adheres to high standards and is better known among researchers than administrators or journalists. A few years ago, I was part of a group of researchers that proposed a method for evaluating global rankings, and the Leiden Ranking was the most preferred of the six we reviewed.

Leiden’s default measurement (which it calls its “traditional edition”) assesses the number of papers over a four-year period in core journals in the Web of Science database. This year, Zhejiang University — not Harvard — is first, and eight of the top 10 institutions are in mainland China.

That is admittedly not the apex of academic publication. Harvard does stay at the top if we consider only the top 10 percent of publications, by citation. If we consider only the top 1 percent most-cited publications, then Harvard is first, and Stanford and Oxford Universities, the University of Toronto, and University College London are in the top 10.

So, when we consider the very small number of massively cited papers, yes, Harvard and Stanford and the traditional U.K. universities are still leading the world. But the trend in science, as in business, is quantity first, and then later quality.

The University Ranking by Academic Performance (URAP) is produced by the Middle East Technical University, in Ankara. It is based entirely on objective public data, provided by the InCites data platform. Here is the most recent overall ranking: first Harvard, and then Université Paris Cité, the University of Toronto, University College London, and Zhejiang. In the 2014-15 rankings the top five went: Harvard, Toronto, Oxford, the Johns Hopkins University, Cambridge. Zhejiang was in 46th place, and the best-performing Asian university was the University of Tokyo, at 17th.

What these rankers consistently capture is that Zhejiang and other Chinese institutions are rising very fast.

If the research tide is turning eastward, why do the “big four” rankings concur in putting Harvard, MIT, Yale, and Stanford at the top, along with Oxford, Cambridge, and one or two of the London colleges?

The answer lies in their methodologies. QS has an academic-reputation survey that has a 30-percent weighting and a survey of employers that accounts for 15 percent. THE has a survey of research and teaching with a weighting of 33 percent, and U.S. News surveys on global and regional research reputation account for a combined 25 percent. These surveys measure perceptions and brand recognition. They are dependent on the perception of achievement over the past decades or even centuries.

The Shanghai Rankings do not have a reputation metric per se, but they do give 20 percent for faculty who win Nobel and Fields awards and 10 percent for alumni who do so, going back several decades.

In addition, THE, QS and U.S. News give priority to citations rather than publications. Citations follow publications and consequently favor the universities that led the research world in the past. The THE world rankings give a 30-percent weighting to research quality, which is based on four indicators that measure citations, and a scant 5.5-percent weight for current research productivity. This difference dismisses the rise of Chinese universities: In the THE world rankings, Tsinghua University, in Beijing, is fifth in the world for research environment — which includes research productivity, research reputation, and research income — but only 60th for research quality, which is based on citations. QS does not count publications at all but has a big weighting for citations per faculty. The U.S. News Best Global Universities has a 10-percent weight for publications and a 50-percent weight for citations.

The rise of China and Asia more generally is accelerating, but that advance is not distributed evenly across the disciplines. China is rapidly taking the lead for research in engineering and computer science. In mathematics and computer-science publications, the entirety of the Leiden Ranking top 30 are Mainland Chinese. Nanyang Technological University, in Singapore, is 34th; the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology is 42nd; the Vellore Institute of Technology, in India, is 44th; and finally, at 50th, there is MIT. If we focus on just the top 1 percent of published research within these fields, it is again Tsinghua in first place, and MIT is 14th.

The message from Leiden is clear. Chinese scientists are pulling ahead of the United States in basic research as measured by publications in the Web of Science. In the harder sciences and in mathematics and computer science, China is surging ahead, continuing a trend that began about two decades ago.

How has this come to pass?

From the 1980s onward, there has been a relentless decline in academic standards in American higher education. Starting in 1994 there was a succession of changes to the SAT that made it more inclusive but perhaps less predictive of future scientific success. Analogies were removed from the verbal section, as were certain advanced topics. Calculators were allowed, and penalties for guessing were eliminated. Further changes came in 2024. Even worse, universities have abandoned standardized testing for undergraduate — and even postgraduate — admissions, to their detriment.

The cognitive skills of American students have been declining for decades, and that decline accelerated in 2020. They do less work, have limited reading skills, and are increasingly intolerant of dissident views. Harvard has had to introduce what is in effect a remedial math course for undergraduate students.

At the same time, the recruitment and promotion of faculty has been seriously compromised. At University of California campuses and other institutions, prospective faculty were until recently subject to political loyalty oaths in the form of diversity statements. In the social sciences and in pharmacology and medical research, there are signs of a widespread crisis of replicability.

In contrast, the leading Chinese universities have maintained rigorously meritocratic policies. No doubt the dreaded Gaokao — the Chinese college-entrance exam — causes an immense amount of stress, but in the current American system, students aiming for elite colleges worry not just about a gruelling test, but about whether their extracurricular activities are sufficiently authentic, their passion sufficiently deep and sustained, whether their big dreams have been transformed into sufficiently bigger realities and whether their essays are exactly what will impress a middling box-checking functionary — or, one suspects, a recently upgraded large language model.

So, the relentless process continues. Every year American researchers produce relatively fewer papers, and their quality declines while Chinese universities produce relatively more papers and more high-quality papers in science and engineering. The process is especially apparent in fields like physics, robotics, and artificial intelligence. And so the scientific world is about to face a dramatic shift in its center of gravity.
